newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Norway crown bubble may soon burst - analysts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Norway crown bubble may soon burst - analysts.

text.p: Speculative money kept on pouring into the Norwegian crown on Monday, sending it to new 52-month highs against the mark but analysts warned that the bubble could soon burst.

"We're in one of those situations where it's not really reacting to fundamentals any more...it's a speculative bubble," said Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase Investment Bank in London.
The crown has gained more than 10 percent against the mark since August -- over half of that since the beginning of 1997.

"I think we're going to have a reversal fairly soon," said Schmidt. "I'm not saying we'll have a change in the medium-term trend, because we probably won't, but this pace of move can't last indefinitely."
The crown soared in morning Europe to 3.8955 per mark -- its best rate since September 1992 and up from late Friday's level of 3.9365 -- though retreated to around 3.9100 by midsession.

"The krona has come such a long way in recent weeks...with most speculative players overweight, that leaves it a little bit exposed to corrective pressures," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell here.
Rising oil prices have been the major driving force behind the crown's sharp appreciation, analysts said.
Norway is the world's second biggest oil exporter after Saudi Arabia, and the market expects huge surpluses in the national budget and current account this year.

But some questioned the wisdom of those assumptions. Not only was the oil price prone to setbacks, making the crown vulnerable, but the non-oil sectors of the economy would suffer from currency strength, they said.

"Perhaps the economy is not as robust as headline growth rates would assume and therefore will not necessarily be able to cope with dramatic appreciation of the exchange rate with total equanimity," said Meggyesi.
Moreover, Chase's Schmidt said there was no massive natural flow into crowns since Norway kept its current account surplus in foreign currency.
The market's current passion for selling marks against all manner of currencies has boosted the crown, but its allied hunt for yield means the crown is not the most obvious choice.
In a vain bid to rein in its soaraway currency, Norway's central bank lowered interest rates twice in two days earlier in January, taking its deposit rate down to just 3.25 percent.
The bank -- which spent tens of billions of crowns on fruitless intervention in the first two weeks of the year -- also said it would let the unit run its course for a while.
Analysts said more rate cuts looked unlikely at present.
"We believe the central bank would rather let the crown appreciate than lower the official rates," said Christiania Markets in a bond market outlook.

Nor is more intervention on the cards right now. "Perhaps the central bank's just biding its time and waiting for when it thinks the market's overextended, and then it can really hurt it. But it doesn't seem to be ready for that yet," said Schmidt.
But while that suggests further near-term crown strength, just how much further it could or should climb is a moot point.

Meggyesi at DMG believes it is already 10 percent overvalued on a Purchasing Power Parity basis, but Wike Groenenberg, senior Scandinavian economist at Salomon Brothers, said the trade-weighted exchange rate was now at fair value.
"My guess is it will probably remain around current levels on a sustained basis," she said.
